engine.what: The RayMakie raster ignores changes to light colour and ambient light unless the screen has gamma set (a display-encoded film), so tinting the sun or moon does nothing in the live dashboard.

An ambient light cannot be added to a RayMakie scene after its first trace ('this scene was first traced without an ambient light, and one cannot be added afterwards'); adding one broke every screenshot.

RayMakie cannot delete! a plot from a traced scene (there is no trace_parts method for RayMakie.RenderObject), and the failed delete leaves the viewport black until a restart, so plugins have to hide plots and keep them forever.

Meshscatter in Hikari/RayMakie does not support per-instance emissive materials: a meshscatter with Hikari.Emission fails in trace_renderobject ('use the single-transform push! for each emitter'), and the game died when a traced frame was rendered after a round of Firefly catch.
Every new SunSkyLight direction re-bakes the sky (about 35 ms), so the sun can only move in 1 degree steps without frame spikes.

engine.what: WGLMakie (the browser view) draws neither shadows nor the SunSkyLight sky, so the browser look is a flatter, different game unless the author fakes sky and water with explicit colours.

process: No. This is the first perfectionist review, so these scores are the baseline. Sixteen sessions added up to 66 minutes of actual author work (.jail/sessions.jsonl: sessions of 1-14 minutes, median about 3, although 45 are allowed), and almost none of it went into anything a player would call content. The loop explains why. session.md step 2 puts 'address open review findings' before any new work, and the per-session reviewer judges only the last diff (does it work, is the text readable, is the evidence complete). So every review produces three to five nits about the previous fix, and those become the next session's work. Name tags were the subject of sessions 1, 2, 3, 4, 10 and 12 and are the plan for session 17; dashboard text wrapping took 11, 12 and 15; firefly crash fixes took 6-8. The night look took 6b, 13 and 14 with nothing visible, because of a raster limit the author should have handed to world/patches after one try. Todo #8 (try the asset pipeline), #4 (movies) and #5 (blog) have been open since the first minute and were never touched. world.json is still the generated starter island, there is one plugin, and no worker job was ever queued, although RULES.md rule 9 says to queue them before breaks. Each short session also pays a fixed cost: re-reading the rules, skills, reviews and todos, and waiting through 1-5 minute game restarts. A third of the daily 3M tokens goes to the reviewer and tester. There is no STYLE.md and no roadmap, so 'the most valuable todo' is whatever the last review complained about; AGENTS.md 'Lessons learned' still reads '(add here)', so lessons stay buried in the journal and get rediscovered. What the loop should make the author do: (1) fewer, longer sessions that use the 45 minutes, each with one content goal from a roadmap of areas, creatures and games (for example 'the beach: pier, boat, shells, a crab mini game'); (2) every session ships at least one thing a player sees in the 3D view (a prop set, an area, a creature, an interaction), and a session without one is a fail unless a crash blocked it; (3) the per-session review blocks only on crashes, regressions and broken features, with at most two findings, and low-severity findings never become todos; polish is batched and judged by this scorecard, with quality.jsonl tracking the scores; (4) write STYLE.md now, and queue 8-12 asset jobs before every break so the worker makes props while no agent runs; (5) time-box engine limits to one attempt, then a patch file and a workaround; (6) move lessons into AGENTS.md, and send test wishes to a test inbox so that 'answer the human first' means the human.

camera.why: The chase cam shows Sprout's blank back with crowns filling 30-40% of the frame, sometimes sits inside a crown; 'free' is frozen because look! runs every frame; follow, orbit and free shots are byte-identical.

creatures.why: The best part: 5 species with googly eyes, cheeks, snoots, wool, jelly, blink, gait and dance code, but on screen they are small pale blobs seen from behind or half hidden by trees; no new species or behaviour in 16 sessions.

fun.why: One mini game with black or invisible fireflies, no direction cue, no feedback on a catch, no best score or reward; no way to touch creatures (click, pet, feed, talk); playing it and then tracing killed the game at 19:46.

lighting.why: One hard sun with near-black core shadows, a flat navy sea, no AO, rim light, fog or coloured shade; 00:43 looks like noon, 19:36 is murky (mean grey 35), night has no moon, stars or warm lights; the traced still is the same picture plus grain.

performance.why: Sim and sync take 1.3 ms median (2.3 ms p95), but the header's '30 fps' leaves out rendering, the last render measurement was p95 42-61 ms, a live screenshot costs 7.6 s, and the game process started 27 times today.

props.why: Four prop types built from unit spheres and cylinders (lollipop trees, three-ball bushes, egg rocks, pin flowers); no catalog.json, the author never ran the asset pipeline, and the first job (by the human's helper) gives an opaque, cropped, photoreal image.

style.why: Glossy toy creatures and primitive props agree as a 'toy box', but there is no STYLE.md, the palette is saturated flat green plus navy, the browser look (no water, no shadows, grey void) is a different game, and the first generated asset is photoreal moss stone.

ui.why: The right third is developer internals (tokens, exit codes, test-wish replies, gamma todos); off-screen names pinned and clipped at the left edge ('umulus', 'ckles', 'oop'); HUD, speech and names pile up in play; the browser view is a fixed 1280x720 figure in a corner.

world.why: Still the generated seed-1 starter island: one round green hill, a sand rim, a flat sea plane, props sprinkled at random; no areas, paths, landmarks, water features, sky or horizon in frame; nothing added in 16 sessions.

summary: A player sees a small toy island: one round, uniformly bright green hill with lollipop trees, egg-shaped rocks and pin flowers. Ten cute but tiny creatures are mostly seen from behind or through tree crowns, and a third of the screen is the developer's token budget, exit codes and replies to automated tests. The only thing to do is a firefly hunt whose fireflies render as black dots or not at all, and after 16 sessions the world is still the generated starter island: the only changes a player would notice are brighter daylight and bigger name tags.
